hook: A coffee shop says 30% of its customers order with its app. You watch 10 random customers and 7 of them use it. Is the shop wrong, or did you see a fluke? When a chance process repeats the same yes-or-no trial a fixed number of times, one formula gives every probability you need to decide.

options: knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other
prereq.why: That is the definition: $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.

figure.caption: The binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.3. The shaded bars, 4 through 10, add to P(X ≥ 4) = 0.350.

chain.cause: A trial has two outcomes and repeats a fixed number of times, independently, with the same p
chain.effect: the count of successes X is binomial with parameters n and p

chain.cause: One order of k successes and n − k failures has probability $p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$
chain.effect: and there are $\binom{n}{k}$ such orders, so $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$

chain.cause: An event like "at least 4" covers several values
chain.effect: add them, or use the complement: $P(X \ge 4) = 1 - P(X \le 3)$

chain.cause: The probability of a result as extreme as the one seen is very small under a claim
chain.effect: the result gives reason to doubt the claim

ideas: A binomial setting: two outcomes per trial, independent trials, a fixed number n of trials, the same success probability p on every trial.
The binomial distribution: $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$.
Show work: name the distribution and parameters, the boundary and the direction: "X is binomial, $n = 10$, $p = 0.3$; $P(X \ge 4) = 1 - P(X \le 3) = 0.350$."
Mean $\mu_X = np$ and standard deviation $\sigma_X = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}$.
Translate carefully: "fewer than 3" is $P(X \le 2)$, "at least 4" is $P(X \ge 4)$.

misconception.right: The complement of "4 or more" is "3 or fewer", so $P(X \ge 4) = 1 - P(X \le 3)$. Subtracting $P(X \le 4)$ throws away the value 4 itself.

summary: When a yes-or-no trial repeats n times independently with the same success probability p, the number of successes is binomial: $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$, with mean np and standard deviation $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$. Name the distribution and its parameters, translate the event into an inequality, and use the complement for "at least" questions. A tiny probability under a claim casts doubt on the claim.
